title: Could silver diamine fluoride help young children avoid dental general anaesthesia?
html:
Dental Tribune International

Tue. 17. November 2026

share save

GREIFSWALD, Germany: In Germany, nearly half of all general anaesthesia procedures in children under 5 are performed for dental indications, and current guidelines recommend pursuing minimally invasive care first. Against this background, researchers at University Medicine Greifswald investigated the outcomes of initiating caries management with silver diamine fluoride (SDF) in children referred for treatment under general anaesthesia. Their findings suggest that this approach may create an opportunity for restorative treatment to be undertaken chairside instead.

In this retrospective study, the researchers reviewed the records for 52 children aged 1–8 who had been referred for possible treatment under general anaesthesia owing to extensive caries and difficulty cooperating during chairside treatment. All received 38% SDF as the starting point of an individualised, minimally invasive pathway that incorporated preventive care, behaviour management and subsequent restorative treatment when necessary.

The analysis covered an average follow-up period of around two years and considered whether the children subsequently underwent dental treatment under general anaesthesia and the clinical success or failure of the SDF-treated teeth. Minor failure was defined as caries progression or reversible pulpitis and major failure as irreversible pulpitis or dental abscess.

Can early caries stabilisation reduce the need for general anaesthesia?

Most of the children were managed without general anaesthesia during follow-up, and the majority of the SDF-treated teeth were classified as clinically successful. No minor failures were documented, although some teeth developed major failures. More than half of the SDF-treated teeth required no subsequent restorative intervention, whereas others received minimally invasive restorative treatment as part of the staged treatment approach.

The authors emphasise that the favourable outcomes should be understood as resulting from the complete treatment approach, as well as the experience of the dental team, rather than SDF alone. They suggest that initial caries stabilisation may give children time to become more cooperative, allowing further care in the dental chair, and that repeated minimally invasive care may gradually improve cooperation through desensitisation and behavioural adaptation.

The findings complement a large US randomised clinical trial previously reported by Dental Tribune International that demonstrated that SDF was more effective than placebo at arresting caries in young children with severe early childhood caries. That trial was designed to support regulatory consideration of SDF for caries arrest—an issue that is also relevant in Europe, where, according to the German researchers, the only SDF-containing product currently available is not formally approved for this indication. The German study provides further insight into its potential role in bridging preventive and restorative paediatric care.

The study, titled “Effect of minimally invasive caries management with silver diammine fluoride on caries progression and subsequent need for dental general anaesthesia in children: A retrospective cohort study”, was published online on 14 November 2026 in Clinical Oral Investigations.
